items.title: Unquoted variables
items.question: A script runs rm -rf $DIR/build and one day DIR is unset. What happens, and how do you guard against it?
items.answer: It expands to rm -rf /build, and unquoted variables also undergo word splitting and glob expansion on spaces or asterisks. Quote every expansion ("$DIR"), use ${DIR:?DIR is not set} to abort when it is empty or unset, and enable set -u to fail on unset variables.

source.name: GNU Bash Manual - Shell Parameter Expansion

items.title: pipefail
items.body: A pipeline returns the exit status of its last command, so failing_cmd | tee log succeeds. set -o pipefail makes it return the status of the rightmost failing command, and the PIPESTATUS array holds every stage's status.

items.title: set -e is not a guarantee
items.question: Why doesn't set -e reliably stop a script on every failure?
items.answer: errexit is ignored in many contexts: commands tested by if or while, commands before && or ||, and non-final pipeline stages without pipefail. It is also suppressed inside functions called from those contexts. Treat it as a safety net and check critical commands explicitly.

source.name: GNU Bash Manual - The Set Builtin

items.title: Pipelines run in subshells
items.body: Each command in a pipeline runs in a subshell by default, so variables changed inside cmd | while read line; do count=$((count+1)); done are lost when the loop ends.
items.question: How do you keep the count?
items.answer: Feed the loop by redirection instead of a pipe: while read -r line; do ...; done < file, or use process substitution: done < <(cmd). Bash also has shopt -s lastpipe, which runs the last stage in the current shell when job control is off.

items.title: Looping over filenames safely
items.question: for f in $(ls *.txt) breaks on filenames containing spaces. What is the robust approach?
items.answer: Iterate the glob directly: for f in ./*.txt; do ...; done, and quote "$f" inside the loop. Command substitution output is word-split on IFS and glob-expanded again. For recursive listings use find ... -print0 with while IFS= read -r -d '' f.

items.title: Cleanup with trap EXIT
items.body: trap 'cleanup' EXIT runs cleanup whenever the shell exits, including after a failure under set -e. It is the standard way to remove temporary files and directories created with mktemp.

source.name: GNU Bash Manual - Bourne Shell Builtins (trap)
